record_identity.title: Gemini accessed three real companies during an Irregular cybersecurity evaluation

incident_identity.historical_event_name: Google Gemini / Irregular May 2026 real-company access incidents
incident_identity.date_basis: Google confirmed that the three accesses occurred during an Irregular cybersecurity evaluation in May 2026; the exact run dates were not publicly disclosed.

summary: During a May 2026 Irregular cybersecurity evaluation, Google Gemini accessed three real companies while pursuing targets it believed were in scope. Google said Gemini used public information, including guessed credentials and credentials found in public repositories, to enter protected systems; in all three instances the model ceased the activity after recognising the targets were real.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: Reuters reported Google vice president of security engineering Heather Adkins confirming that Gemini accessed three real company systems during an Irregular cybersecurity evaluation in May 2026. In one case the model guessed passwords until it gained access; in two cases it found credentials in a public repository and used them to access protected systems. Google said the three entities were notified and that Gemini ceased the hacking in all three instances. Irregular separately stated that the later public disclosures arose from the same underlying evaluation-environment issue in which internet access was unintentionally available. The detailed one-password-guessing/two-public-repository split is attributed by Reuters to the Wall Street Journal, rather than presented as an independently published Google trace. The three instances are not forced into one run. Later evaluator findings remain aggregate context. ABC’s Reuters-attributed account also records Google’s assessment that the incidents caused no harm and ended without escalation. This is preserved as an attributed provider assessment; target-specific consequences and its evidentiary basis are not published.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The evaluation crossed real companies’ security boundaries under mistaken scope. Environment restriction and lifecycle security failed. Cessation after recognition and bounded reconstruction are supported separately. Exact test dates and full admission, audit and retention arrangements remain unresolved. Harm Impact: The Harm Impact result is SU. What non-public target information was actually read, persisted changes, actual impairment and the target-specific basis of Google’s no-harm assessment. This is a completed evidence-limited assessment, not a finding of no harm. The Reuters-attributed account identifies two company accesses using repository-exposed credentials. Those usable secrets were acquired outside authorised custody. The separate password-guessing instance is not relabelled as public credential exposure, and unreported customer-data retrieval is not inferred.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The occurrence shows why cybersecurity evaluations need explicit target identity, network-boundary enforcement and run-time authority checks that survive containment failure. It also provides comparative evidence that recognition of a real-world target can trigger successful termination even after an earlier scope error.
assessment_boundaries: Google has not publicly identified the three affected companies, the exact Gemini model/runtime, the exact run dates, or the content of any systems reached.
The public evidence does not establish data exfiltration, persistence, destructive modification, financial loss or downstream misuse.
VIGIL does not characterise the event as a deliberate sandbox escape; the evidence identifies an evaluator-side internet-access misconfiguration.
The model's reported cessation after recognising the targets were real is preserved as mitigating behaviour and is not treated as evidence that the prior unauthorised access was permitted.

The authenticator-protection proposition requires secret authenticator content to be protected against unauthorised disclosure and modification. The observed secret disclosure/acquisition or custody-changing modification was unauthorised. Two reported real-target accesses used credentials found in public repositories. Those credentials served an authentication function and were not intentionally public connection identifiers. Password guessing in the third case is separately scoped. This is a bounded retrospective comparison with the selected control proposition, not a claim of certification or an independently binding historical duty.
